leads.caseName: Wilmington Trust, N.A. v. Stradtman Park, LLC
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Wilmington Trust, N.A. v Stradtman Park, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05883 
 October 9, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 WILMINGTON TRUST, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION, AS TRUSTEE FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE REGISTERED HOLDERS OF JPMBB COMMERCIAL MORTGAGE SECURITIES TRUST 2014-C24, COMMERCIAL MORTGAGE PASS-THROUGH CERTIFICATES, SERIES 2014-C24, BY AND THROUGH ITS SPECIAL SERVICER, LNR PARTNERS, LLC, PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT, 
 v 
 STRADTMAN PARK, LLC, DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT, ET AL., DEFENDANTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 9, 2026 
 643 CA 25-01133 
 Present: Lindley, J.P., Curran, Ogden, Delconte, And Hannah, JJ. 

 MCCARTER & ENGLISH, LLP, NEW YORK CITY (GREGORY J. MASCITTI OF COUNSEL), FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT. 
 THE SAGE LAW FIRM GROUP PLLC, BUFFALO (KATHRYN FRIEDMAN OF COUNSEL), FOR DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT. 

 Appeal from an amended order and judgment of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Emilio Colaiacovo, J.), entered May 21, 2025, in a mortgage foreclosure action. The amended order and judgment, inter alia, granted plaintiff money damages. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the amended order and judgment so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs. 
 Memorandum: In July 2014, defendant Stradtman Park, LLC (defendant) executed a loan agreement, promissory note, and mortgage and various other documents (loan documents) with nonparty KeyBank National Association (KeyBank) pursuant to which defendant obtained a $3.6 million loan on a commercial property valued at approximately $7 million. The loan documents permitted KeyBank to reassign the loan and to permit securitization through a commercial mortgage-backed security (CMBS) and required defendant to make certain modifications to the loan as required to facilitate the securitization. 
 In October 2014, KeyBank assigned the loan to plaintiff, Wilmington Trust, National Association, as Trustee for the benefit of the registered holders of JPMBB Commercial Mortgage Securities Trust 2014-C24, Commercial Mortgage Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2014-C24 (plaintiff), which placed the loan into a CMBS pursuant to a pooling and servicing agreement (PSA). It is undisputed that defendant was not a signatory to the PSA, and defendant asserts that it was not provided a copy of that document until after this litigation commenced. Pursuant to the PSA, LNR Partners, LLC (LNR) was to act as the special servicer of the loan in the event that defendant's loan became distressed or in default. 
 From 2014 through early 2020, defendant paid all amounts required by the loan documents. Specifically, defendant was required to pay principal and interest in the amount of $18,779.30 per month and reserve account payments, which were funds for taxes, insurance, maintenance, repairs, etc., in the amount of $20,300.39 per month, for a monthly total payment of $39,079.69. 
 At some point in 2019, defendant requested approval for lease renewals, expansions, contractor repair payments, and other relief required to be paid from the reserve accounts [*2] pursuant to the loan documents. Although the loan was neither distressed nor in default, LNR became the contact entity for such requests. According to defendant, LNR was dilatory and obstructionist with all of defendant's legitimate requests and, as a result, defendant was forced to pay certain amounts itself, despite having ample reserve funds to make those payments. 
 Defendant began paying only the principal and interest on the loan in May 2020 and withheld the reserve amounts, directing that its monthly payments of $18,779.30 be applied toward principal and interest only. Plaintiff or LNR, however, spread those payments over principal, interest, and reserve payments, resulting in defendant's default. In November 2020, defendant stopped remitting the rental payment proceeds required by the loan documents to plaintiff, which later commenced this action seeking, inter alia, to foreclose on the mortgage. 
 Supreme Court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment with respect to the first and third causes of action, i.e., mortgage foreclosure and entitlement to rents. That order is not challenged on appeal. Questioning many of the fees sought to be recovered by plaintiff, the court directed a hearing on damages. Plaintiff appeals from the subsequent amended order and judgment, contending that the court erred in its determinations with respect to certain damages and fees. We now affirm. 
 At hearings or inquests regarding damages, "the plaintiff bears the burden of setting forth a prima facie case as to damages" ( Bobbo Prop. Mgt. , Inc. v Faulkner , 235 AD3d 615 , 615 [2d Dept 2025]; see Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy. , FSB v Moriarty-Gentile , 242 AD3d 1150 , 1152 [2d Dept 2025]), and, on an appeal from a nonjury hearing or trial, "this Court 'has authority . . . as broad as that of the trial court . . . and . . . may render the judgment it finds warranted by the facts' . . . 'Nonetheless, the decision of the fact-finding court should not be disturbed upon appeal unless it is obvious that the court's conclusions could not be reached under any fair interpretation of the evidence' " ( DiMarco Constructors , LLC v Top Capital of N.Y. Brockport , LLC , 236 AD3d 1342 , 1343 [4th Dept 2025]; see Estate of Sonnelitter v Estate of White [appeal No. 2], 115 AD3d 1160, 1162 [4th Dept 2014]). 
 Although there is a " 'sound rule in the construction of contracts, that where the language is clear, unequivocal and unambiguous, the contract is to be interpreted by its own language' " ( R/S Assoc. v New York Job Dev. Auth ., 98 NY2d 29, 32 [2002], quoting Springsteen v Samson , 32 NY 703 , 706 [1865]), we note that " '[a] foreclosure action is equitable in nature and triggers the equitable powers of the court' . . . '[O]nce equity is invoked, the court's power is as broad as equity and justice require' " ( Meadowlands Portfolio , LLC v Manton , 118 AD3d 1439, 1440 [4th Dept 2014]; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Losner , 145 AD3d 935, 938 [2d Dept 2016]). 
 Here, plaintiff contends that the court erred in denying it recovery of note rate interest in the amount of $120,882.59, in addition to the default rate interest of $583,938.25 awarded by the court. Contrary to plaintiff's contention, it was not entitled to both note rate interest and default rate interest inasmuch as the default rate was set at five percent above the note rate and the court awarded plaintiff the exact amount of default rate interest it requested. Because plaintiff did not establish with documentary evidence how the default rate interest it requested was calculated, we conclude that the court's determination that it would be duplicative to award both default rate interest and note rate interest is supported by a fair interpretation of the evidence. 
 We reject plaintiff's further contention that the court abused its discretion in determining the amount of the attorneys' fees awarded. Defendant did not dispute that plaintiff and LNR were entitled to attorneys' fees, but it contested the reasonableness of the requested fees, relying on expert testimony regarding reasonable fees for commercial mortgage foreclosure actions in Western New York. Defendant's expert opined that a "customary, reasonable" fee for an experienced attorney in commercial foreclosure proceedings in Western New York would range from $350 to $450 an hour. Plaintiff's sole witness testified that LNR was paying between $650-800 an hour for the services of law firm partners and between $350-575 an hour for associates. None of the attorney invoices submitted by plaintiff delineated the rate for each charge. Plaintiff requested approximately $588,000 in attorneys' fees, but the court awarded only $250,000, finding that the rates requested by plaintiff were unreasonable and that numerous charges were "duplicative and exaggerated." Indeed, the court noted that plaintiff had come "perilously close" to having the entire judgment vacated due to its exorbitant request for attorneys' fees. 
 An award of attorneys' fees, even if permitted by contract, " 'may only be enforced to the extent that the amount is reasonable and warranted for the services actually rendered' " ( SO/Bluestar , LLC v Canarsie Hotel Corp ., 33 AD3d 986, 987 [2d Dept 2006]). Such a determination involves a review of the number of hours spent on the case, the hourly rate that was being charged, and the customary fees charged for services by lawyers in the community with like experience and reputation ( see Matakov v Kel-Tech Constr. Inc ., 84 AD3d 677, 678 [1st Dept 2011]; Wells v Crosson , 210 AD2d 932, 932 [4th Dept 1994]; Getty Petroleum Corp. v G.M. Triple S. Corp ., 187 AD2d 483, 483-484 [2d Dept 1992]). We conclude that the court's determination to award $250,000 was not an abuse of discretion and should not be disturbed. 
 We have reviewed plaintiff's remaining challenges to the court's determinations with respect to the awards of damages and fees and conclude that all the challenged determinations are based on a fair interpretation of the evidence and that none of those challenges warrants modification or reversal of the amended order and judgment. 
 Entered: October 9, 2026 
 Ann Dillon Flynn 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Security First Insurance Company D/B/A Security First Florida v. Mark Annon and Amy Annon
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
FIFTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL
 STATE OF FLORIDA
 _____________________________

 Case No. 5D2025-1458
 LT Case No. 2021-CA-000558
 _____________________________

SECURITY FIRST INSURANCE
COMPANY D/B/A SECURITY FIRST
FLORIDA,

 Appellant,

 v.

MARK ANNON AND AMY ANNON,

 Appellees.
 _____________________________

On appeal from the Circuit Court for Flagler County.
Andrea K. Totten, Judge.

Michael Fox Orr and Loreyn P. Raab, of Orr Cook, Jacksonville,
for Appellant.

Michael Ciocchetti, of Michael Ciocchetti, PLLC, Daytona Beach,
for Appellee.

 October 9, 2026

LAMBERT, J.

 Security First Insurance Company (“Security First”), which
was the defendant below in a first-party property dispute that was
resolved without a trial, timely appeals the trial court’s
subsequent final judgment that awarded attorney’s fees against it
 under section 627.428, Florida Statutes (2021), 1 in favor of the
appellees/insureds, Mark Annon and Amy Annon. Consistent with
Florida Patient’s Compensation Fund v. Rowe, 472 So. 2d 1145
(Fla. 1985), the trial court first computed and then awarded to
Appellees in its final judgment the lodestar amount of $125,080.00
for attorney’s fees, which Security First has not challenged in this
appeal. The court then applied a 2.0 contingency fee multiplier to
this lodestar figure, resulting in an attorney’s fees award to
Appellees totaling $250,160.00, with which Security First does
take issue.

 Security First primarily argues that the 2.0 multiplier award
should be reversed because it is not supported by competent
substantial evidence. Concluding that Security First is correct, we
reverse the final judgment and remand with instructions to the
trial court to enter an amended final judgment that awards the
lodestar attorney’s fees sum of $125,080.00 to Appellees, without
a multiplier.
 I

 In Standard Guaranty Insurance v. Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d
828 (Fla. 1990), the Florida Supreme Court set forth the following
three factors to be utilized by courts when determining whether a
multiplier is necessary in the instant type of case:

 (1) whether the relevant market requires a
 contingency fee multiplier to obtain competent
 counsel; (2) whether the attorney was able to mitigate
 the risk of nonpayment in any way; and (3) whether
 any of the factors set forth in Rowe are applicable,
 especially, the amount involved, the results obtained,
 and the type of fee arrangement between the attorney
 and [the] client.

Id. at 834.

 1 Section 627.428, Florida Statutes, which permitted an award

of attorney’s fees in this type of case, was repealed in 2023. The
claim in this case pre-dates the repeal.

 2
  As the party seeking attorney’s fees, Appellees had the
burden to establish each of these factors to justify the contingency
fee multiplier. See Foot & Ankle Ctr. of Fla., LLC, v. Vargas, 412
So. 3d 825, 828 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024) (citing Quanstrom, 555 So. 2d
at 834). And “[w]hile the trial court’s determination to apply a
multiplier to the lodestar amount is reviewed for an abuse of
discretion, the trial court’s findings as to the multiplier must be
supported by competent, substantial evidence.” Universal Prop. &
Cas. Ins. v. Deshpande, 314 So. 3d 416, 420 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)
(citation omitted).

 II

 In arguing that the trial court’s application of the 2.0
contingency fee multiplier was not supported by competent
substantial evidence, Security First contends that Appellees failed
to meet their burden of presenting evidence sufficient to prove that
the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to obtain
competent counsel in this case. See SafePoint Ins. v. Castellanos,
394 So. 3d 731, 735 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (“If there is no evidence
that the relevant market required a contingency fee multiplier to
obtain competent counsel, then a multiplier should not be
awarded.” (citation omitted)).

 Security First also contends that the trial court’s finding on
the second prong or factor in Quanstrom, that Appellees’ counsel
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way, lacks
record evidentiary support.

 To establish the first factor under Quanstrom, Appellees
were required to demonstrate, without inference, that they would
have faced substantial difficulties in obtaining competent counsel
in the relevant market without the risk-enhancement multiplier.
See Little v. Bath & Kitchen Boutique, LLC, 435 So. 3d 1142, 1150
(Fla. 3d DCA 2026) (citing Foot & Ankle, 412 So. 3d at 829).

 Appellees did not testify at the attorney’s fees hearing; and
their expert witness, who admitted under oath that he did not
handle first-party property insurance cases such as the instant
claim nor did he speak with Appellees, testified that he made no
inquiry as to whether any other attorneys would have accepted

 3
 this type of case without the possibility of a contingency fee
multiplier. See Impex Caribe Corp. v. Carl Levin, P.A., 338 So. 3d
13, 15 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (recognizing that the party seeking
application of the multiplier “must establish ‘that a party would
have difficulty securing counsel without the opportunity for a
multiplier’” (quoting Citizens Prop. Ins. v. Laguerre, 259 So. 3d
169, 177 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018))); see also Bankers Life & Cas. v.
Borew, 430 So. 3d 124, 128 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (“So, to award the
multiplier, the record evidence must show that without risk-
enhancement[,] plaintiff would have faced substantial difficulties
in finding counsel in the . . . relevant market.” (alteration in
original) (citation omitted)).

 Instructive on this issue is this court’s decision in PHH
Mortgage Corp. v. Schreiber, 397 So. 3d 1159 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024),
where the appellant challenged an attorney’s fees award with a
contingency fee multiplier in a foreclosure case. Id. at 1159. The
appellees’ expert there testified that for “almost all [foreclosure]
clients, because they couldn’t pay their mortgage, they can’t pay
their attorney or . . . they pay very little as compared to the amount
of work involved.” Id. at 1160 (alteration in original). The expert
further opined that, because of the client’s inability to pay, most
foreclosures involved some type of contingency fee. Id.

 Concluding that this testimony said nothing about whether a
foreclosure client could have obtained competent counsel without
a multiplier, we reversed and remanded for entry of an amended
judgment without the contingency multiplier. Id.

 Appellees’ expert’s testimony here was similarly lacking as to
whether Appellees could have obtained competent counsel in the
relevant market absent the possibility of a multiplier. We
therefore hold, without further elaboration, that Appellees failed
to meet their evidentiary burden under the first Quanstrom factor
to support the imposition of the contingency risk multiplier.

 III

 We further find that Appellees did not present competent
substantial evidence of the second Quanstrom factor that counsel
was unable to mitigate the risk of nonpayment in any way.

 4
 “Generally, the controlling consideration in determining whether
an attorney can mitigate the risk of nonpayment . . . is whether the
plaintiffs can afford a retainer or hourly fees.” Certain
Underwriters at Lloyd’s London v. Candelaria, 339 So. 3d 463, 470
(Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (quoting Wesson v. Fla. Peninsula Ins., 296 So.
3d 572, 573 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020)). Simply stated, there was no
specific, non-inferential evidence before the trial court that
Appellees could not have afforded or lacked the financial means to
either pay a retainer fee or counsel’s hourly rate.

 Accordingly, we conclude that the trial court erred in applying
the 2.0 contingency risk multiplier to the lodestar attorney’s fees
amount. We therefore reverse that portion of the final judgment
and remand with directions to the trial court to enter an amended
final judgment that awards to Appellees the $125,080.00 lodestar
attorney’s fees figure previously determined, with no multiplier. 2

 REVERSED and REMANDED with directions.

EDWARDS and BOATWRIGHT, JJ., concur.

 2 On a final note, effective March 24, 2023, the Florida
Legislature amended section 57.104, Florida Statutes, to provide
that “[i]n any action in which attorney fees are determined or
awarded by the court, there is a strong presumption that a lodestar
fee is sufficient and reasonable,” and that “[t]his presumption may
be overcome only in a rare and exceptional circumstance with
evidence that competent counsel could not otherwise be retained.”
§ 57.104(2), Fla. Stat. Security First’s second argument for
reversal here briefly argued that this statute should be applied
retroactively and that this was not the rare and exceptional case
to overcome the strong presumption that the lodestar fee awarded
was sufficient and reasonable.

 While the record in this appeal supports Security First’s
argument that this case was not rare and exceptional, based upon
our disposition of Security First’s first issue on appeal, we find it
unnecessary to address the retroactive applicability of section
57.104(2).

 5
  _____________________________

Not final until disposition of any timely and
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or
9.331.
